claim: The subthalamic nucleus (STN) is composed principally of excitatory projection neurons.
source: The STN is composed principally of excitatory projection neurons (Barroso-Chinea et al., 2007; Hammond et al., 1978; Smith and Parent, 1988).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published studies.

claim: The STN serves as a key node along the striatal indirect pathway, receiving inhibitory input via the external segment of the globus pallidus (GPe).
source: It serves as a key node along the striatal indirect pathway, receiving inhibitory input via the external segment of the globus pallidus (GPe) (Magill et al., 2004; Parent and Hazrati, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies.

claim: The STN projects broadly within the basal ganglia, sending dense projections to the internal globus pallidus (in rodents called entopeduncular nucleus, EP), substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr), and reciprocal projections to GPe.
source: The STN projects broadly within the basal ganglia, sending dense projections to the internal globus pallidus (in rodents called entopeduncular nucleus, EP), substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr), and reciprocal projections to GPe.
evidence: This is stated as established anatomical knowledge without specific citation in this sentence.

claim: In primates, damage to the STN is associated with uncontrolled voluntary movements (hemiballismus).
source: In primates, damage to the STN is associated with uncontrolled voluntary movements (hemiballismus) (Hamada and DeLong, 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: In rodents, genetic disruption of excitatory output from the STN via partial knockout of the vesicular glutamate transporter 2 (VGLUT2) induces hyperlocomotion.
source: In rodents, genetic disruption of excitatory output from the STN via partial knockout of the vesicular glutamate transporter 2 (VGLUT2) induces hyperlocomotion (Schweizer et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: STN lesions in rodents induce impulsive responding.
source: lesions induce impulsive responding (Baunez and Robbins, 1997; Eagle et al., 2008; Uslaner and Robinson, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published studies.

claim: The STN is activated by signals to stop an initiated response as shown by human fMRI.
source: For example, the STN is activated by signals to stop an initiated response as shown by human fMRI (Aron and Poldrack, 2006)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: The STN is activated by the need to delay responding during conflict.
source: The STN is also activated by the need to delay responding during conflict (reviewed by Zavala et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: The STN is activated in response to surprising events.
source: The STN is also activated by the need to delay responding during conflict (reviewed by Zavala et al., 2015) or in response to surprising events (Wessel et al., 2016b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: When stop signals, conflict signals, or surprising events recruit the STN it activates basal ganglia output nuclei, transiently inhibiting thalamocortical drive.
source: Anatomical and computational models propose that when stop signals, conflict signals, or surprising events recruit the STN it activates basal ganglia output nuclei, transiently inhibiting thalamocortical drive (Bogacz and Gurney, 2007; Mink, 1996; Wiecki and Frank, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published studies describing anatomical and computational models.

claim: STN lesions affected behavior in stop signal tasks, but the effects were modest and not specific to stopping.
source: While STN lesions did affect behavior in stop signal tasks, the effects were modest and not specific to stopping (Eagle et al., 2008; Obeso et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies.

claim: ChR2:YFP or YFP alone was expressed in STN glutamate cells using Slc17a6-Cre (VGLUT2-Cre) knock-in mice and AAV vectors.
source: Using Slc17a6-Cre (VGLUT2-Cre) knock-in mice and Adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors we expressed Channelrhodopsin-2 fused with yellow fluorescent protein (ChR2:YFP) or YFP alone (control) in STN glutamate cells.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Dense YFP label was observed in STN and its major terminal regions including the GPe, EP, and SNr, with some spread to the parasubthalamic nucleus and the ventromedial thalamus.
source: We observed dense YFP label in STN (Figure 1A) and its major terminal regions including the GPe (Figure 1B), EP (Figure 1C), and SNr (Figure 1D), with some spread to the parasubthalamic nucleus and the ventromedial thalamus.
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1A-D.

claim: STN neurons expressing ChR2 increased firing in response to 10 ms flashes of blue light at 40 Hz.
source: Cell-attached recordings showed that STN neurons expressing ChR2 increased firing in response to 10 ms flashes of blue light at 40 Hz (Figure 1E)
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In both ChR2 stimulation experiments, firing persisted for the duration of the stimulus, followed by apparent brief rebound inhibition.
source: In both experiments firing persisted for the duration of the stimulus, followed by apparent brief rebound inhibition.
evidence: This is an observation from the electrophysiological data presented in Figure 1E and 1F.

claim: Light-evoked excitatory post-synaptic currents (EPSCs) were observed in postsynaptic cells juxtaposed to fluorescent ChR2-expressing STN terminals in the GPe, EP, and SNr.
source: To test connectivity, we next recorded light-evoked responses from post-synaptic cells juxtaposed to fluorescent ChR2-expressing STN terminals in the GPe, EP, and SNr –revealing excitatory post-synaptic currents (EPSCs) in each of these targets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: EPSCs assessed pharmacologically showed DNQX sensitivity, confirming broad glutamate-mediated postsynaptic effects.
source: EPSCs that were assessed pharmacologically showed DNQX sensitivity, confirming broad glutamate-mediated postsynaptic effects (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: 40 Hz stimulation for 5 s of STN inputs resulted in a mean 2- to 4-fold increase in firing in GPe, EP, and SNr.
source: To test whether stimulation of STN inputs could increase firing in postsynaptic targets we applied 40 Hz stimulation for 5 s while recording action potentials from GPe, EP, and SNr, observing a mean 2- to 4-fold increase in firing in each region (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–G.

claim: Photostimulus trains applied 90 min prior to sacrifice using either 0.5 mW or 10 mW light led to robust Fos expression in STN.
source: Finally, to ensure our targeting strategy was effective in activating STN neurons and their postsynaptic partners in vivo, photostimulus trains were applied 90 min prior to sacrifice using either 0.5 mW or 10 mW light. This led to robust Fos expression in STN (Figure 1G–I)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 1G–I.

claim: Unilateral STN photostimulation (10 mW, 10 pulses, 40 Hz) in ChR2-expressing mice caused a significant increase in the number of bouts containing precisely two licks.
source: Unilateral STN photostimulation (10 mW, 10 pulses, 40 Hz) in ChR2-expressing mice caused a significant increase in the number of bouts containing precisely two licks (Figure 2C)
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Similar results to 10 mW stimulation were observed using 20-fold less power (0.5 mW) or with bilateral stimulation.
source: Similar results were observed using 20-fold less power (0.5 mW) or with bilateral stimulation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: A single 50 ms pulse delivered subsequent to the second lick in a bout showed the same effect as the 10 pulse train.
source: Strikingly, a single 50 ms pulse delivered subsequent to the second lick in a bout showed the same effect (Figure 2D,G and Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2D,G and Video 1.

claim: When 50 ms stimulation was triggered by the second lick but did not provoke interruption, there was a rightward shift in the inter-lick interval (ILI) distribution between the second and third licks.
source: Further, when assessing the subset of bouts where 50 ms stimulation was triggered by the second lick but did not provoke interruption, we found a rightward shift in the inter-lick interval (ILI) distribution between the second and third licks (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: STN activation reduces the occurrence of licks with ILIs between 100–200 ms.
source: In particular, STN activation reduces the occurrence of licks with ILIs between 100–200 ms (Figure 2I)
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Laser-mediated STN inhibition on its own induced no change in lick pattern.
source: To determine whether laser-mediated STN inhibition on its own induced any effects on licking, the second lick in a bout triggered a 1 s green laser pulse; we saw no change in lick pattern (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F,G.

claim: Surprise (without laser) interrupted licking, increasing the proportion of bouts with <3 licks for both YFP- and Halo-expressing groups.
source: As expected, surprise (without laser) interrupted licking, increasing the proportion of bouts with <3 licks for both YFP- and Halo-expressing groups (Figure 3E)
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: On bouts where surprise was preceded by laser, there was a reduction in the number of short bouts in the Halo group compared to YFP control mice.
source: Critically, however, on bouts where surprise was preceded by laser, we found a reduction in the number of short bouts in the Halo group compared to YFP control mice (Figure 3E and Video 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3E and Video 3.

claim: STN inhibition blunted the interruptive effects of surprise across several similar experiments and multiple cohorts.
source: This effect was observed repeatedly, with STN inhibition blunting the interruptive effects of surprise across several similar experiments and multiple cohorts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Brief activation of STN projection neurons was sufficient to interrupt or pause a self-initiated bout of licking.
source: Next we showed that brief activation of STN projection neurons was sufficient to interrupt or pause a self-initiated bout of licking.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the experimental findings presented in Figure 2.

claim: STN inhibition reduced the disruptive effect of surprise.
source: Finally, we developed an assay in which surprise was used to interrupt licking, and showed that STN inhibition reduced the disruptive effect of surprise.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the experimental findings presented in Figure 3.

claim: STN activation interrupts behavior.
source: Thus STN activation interrupts behavior
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Blocking the STN blunts the interruptive effect of surprise.
source: blocking the STN blunts the interruptive effect of surprise.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The STN is both necessary and sufficient for behavioral response suppression.
source: These results provide strong evidence that the STN is both necessary and sufficient for such forms of behavioral response suppression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental data showing both sufficiency (ChR2 activation) and necessity (Halo inhibition).

claim: A lick bout was defined as two or more licks with <750 ms inter-lick intervals, which included >92% of all licks from spontaneously licking mice.
source: We defined a bout as two or more licks with <750 ms inter-lick intervals, which included >92% of all licks from spontaneously licking mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a methodological definition supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was a significant shift toward longer IBI length following STN-induced behavioral interruption.
source: We also examined the inter-bout interval (IBI), comparing the interval between bouts following laser trials versus non-laser trials. We found a significant shift toward longer IBI length following STN-induced behavioral interruption (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: The ChR2 group showed a (presumably compensatory) increase in the number of self-initiated bouts and licks.
source: Importantly, the ChR2 group showed no reduction but rather a (presumably compensatory) increase in the number of self-initiated bouts and licks (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F,G)
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F,G.

claim: Behavioral interruption is not explained by an aversive effect.
source: suggesting that behavioral interruption is not explained by an aversive effect.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that ChR2 mice showed increased bouts and licks.

claim: STN stimulation rapidly and potently interrupts or pauses licking in a manner consistent with implementing a behavioral stop/pause.
source: Thus, STN stimulation rapidly and potently interrupts or pauses licking in a manner consistent with implementing a behavioral stop/pause.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Surprising events activate the STN.
source: We hypothesized that because surprising events activate the STN (Wessel et al., 2016b)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Surprising events interrupt licking.
source: We hypothesized that because surprising events activate the STN (Wessel et al., 2016b) and interrupt licking (O'Connor et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: When triggered by the second lick in a bout, the surprising event potently interrupted behavior in untreated mice.
source: A pilot experiment on untreated mice showed that, when triggered by the second lick in a bout, the surprising event potently interrupted behavior
evidence: This is a description of pilot experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mice habituated to the surprising event over the course of several sessions as would be expected by the waning of surprise.
source: moreover, mice habituated over the course of several sessions as would be expected by the waning of surprise (Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and Video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and Video 2.

claim: STN inhibition reduced the disruptive effect of surprise on licking behavior.
source: These data show that STN inhibition reduced the disruptive effect of surprise on licking behavior, indicating that STN activity is necessary for normal surprise-induced interruption.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: STN activity is necessary for normal surprise-induced interruption.
source: These data show that STN inhibition reduced the disruptive effect of surprise on licking behavior, indicating that STN activity is necessary for normal surprise-induced interruption.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of the STN, delivered after the second lick in a bout, rapidly interrupted or paused licking.
source: We showed that optogenetic stimulation of the STN, delivered after the second lick in a bout, rapidly interrupted or paused licking.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the experimental findings.

claim: The interruption occurred even when the optogenetic stimulation was brief (50 ms) or delivered at low power (0.5 mW).
source: The interruption occurred even when the optogenetic stimulation was brief (50 ms) or delivered at low power (0.5 mW)
evidence: This is a summary statement of the experimental findings.

claim: Behavior can be rapidly and potently interrupted by transient increases in STN output.
source: supporting the specificity of this manipulation and suggesting that behavior can be rapidly and potently interrupted by transient increases in STN output.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: STN inhibition in the Halo-expressing mice strongly and reproducibly mitigated the interruptive effects of surprise on licking when compared to YFP-expressing control mice.
source: Second, STN inhibition in the Halo-expressing mice strongly and reproducibly mitigated the interruptive effects of surprise on licking when compared to YFP-expressing control mice.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the experimental findings.

claim: Absent surprise, 1 s STN inhibition did not alter licking behavior.
source: Importantly, absent surprise, 1 s STN inhibition did not alter licking behavior
evidence: This is a summary statement of the experimental findings.

claim: Previous studies link STN lesions to hemiballismus and dyskinesia.
source: this despite previous studies linking STN lesions to hemiballismus and dyskinesia (Hamada and DeLong, 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Involuntary movements result from the sustained rather than acute loss of STN output, perhaps due to compensatory changes in basal ganglia circuitry.
source: These observations suggest that involuntary movements result from the sustained rather than acute loss of STN output, perhaps due to compensatory changes in basal ganglia circuitry.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Acute STN activation interrupts behavior.
source: In sum, our data demonstrate that acute STN activation interrupts behavior
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Acutely blocking the STN diminishes the impact of surprise on behavior.
source: and acutely blocking the STN diminishes the impact of surprise on behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The results provide causal evidence of a role for the STN in stopping/pausing.
source: Together, these data provide causal evidence of a role for the STN in stopping/pausing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The results validate a large empirical literature showing that STN activity is elicited by stop signals, switch signals, and decision conflict.
source: The results validate a large empirical literature showing that STN activity is elicited by stop signals, switch signals, and decision conflict (Wessel and Aron, 2017; Jahanshahi et al., 2015; Wiecki and Frank, 2013; Zavala et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data, supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Increased STN activity in response to stop signals, switch signals, and decision conflict observed in previous studies is not epiphenomenal, or correlated with some other variable such as arousal or effort, but instead reflects an implementation of stopping/pausing driven by STN recruitment.
source: Our data strongly suggest that increased STN activity in response to such signals observed in previous studies is not epiphenomenal, or correlated with some other variable such as arousal or effort, but instead reflects an implementation of stopping/pausing driven by STN recruitment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Much previous work on the role of the STN in response inhibition tested its role on pre-potent actions, prior to the initiation of action.
source: Note that much previous work on the role of the STN in response inhibition tested its role on pre-potent actions, prior to the initiation of action, for example using Go/NoGo or stop-signal tasks.
evidence: This is a statement about the existing literature.

claim: The current study assessed the effect of the STN on a recently initiated action sequence, ~100–300 ms after the measurement of an action (lick bout), instead of before it.
source: Here, however, we assessed the effect of the STN on a recently initiated action sequence, ~100–300 ms after the measurement of an action (lick bout), instead of before it.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: STN activity can inhibit an ongoing action.
source: In other words, we found that STN activity can inhibit an ongoing action
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The study did not directly test the STN's role in inhibiting action initiation.
source: but we did not directly test its role in inhibiting action initiation.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the study.

claim: An STN-driven system for Stopping or Pausing in response to surprise or conflict signals has ethological utility whether a new action sequence is being initiated, or is already underway.
source: We suppose that an STN-driven system for Stopping or Pausing in response to surprise or conflict signals, to interrupt or delay an action plan in order to consider new evidence, has ethological utility whether a new action sequence is being initiated, or is already underway.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Recent studies have linked STN-mediated stopping to working memory decrements.
source: Recent studies have linked STN-mediated stopping to working memory decrements (Wessel et al., 2016b)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: There are neural circuit links between stopping behavior and cognition.
source: Recent studies have linked STN-mediated stopping to working memory decrements (Wessel et al., 2016b), suggesting neural circuit links between stopping behavior and cognition.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited study.

claim: Excess and aberrant activity in the STN may induce a pathological state of stopping and interruption.
source: Further, excess and aberrant activity in the STN may induce a pathological state of stopping and interruption
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Excess and aberrant activity in the STN may explain why STN lesions or deep brain stimulation dramatically improve Parkinsonian motor deficits.
source: excess and aberrant activity in the STN may induce a pathological state of stopping and interruption, and explain why STN lesions or deep brain stimulation dramatically improve Parkinsonian motor deficits (Brittain et al., 2014; Wichmann et al., 2011).

claim: Brief activation of the STN is sufficient to interrupt or pause behavior.
source: By providing causal evidence that brief activation of the STN is sufficient to interrupt or pause behavior

claim: STN activity contributes to surprise-induced behavioral interruption.
source: and that STN activity contributes to surprise-induced behavioral interruption

claim: The current results put the functional role of the STN on a much firmer footing.
source: the current results put the functional role of the STN on a much firmer footing.
